meta.title: Operation of Digital Photoactometer in Pharmacology Laboratory

sections.purpose: To quantify spontaneous locomotor activity in rodents (mice/rats) using light beam interruption technology for evaluation of CNS stimulant and depressant drugs in experimental pharmacology.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacology laboratory for assessment of drug effects on motor activity, sedation screening, psychostimulant evaluation, and CNS drug profiling as per standard pharmacological methods.
procedure: Switch on the digital photoactometer and allow it to complete the self-test sequence.
Confirm the display shows zero counts before starting.
Clean the activity chamber with 70% ethanol and allow to dry completely — residual odour from previous animals affects behaviour of the test animal.
Acclimatize the laboratory animal (mouse: 20–25 g; rat: 150–200 g) to the laboratory environment for 30–60 minutes before the experiment.
Administer the test drug or vehicle control by the specified route (oral, i.p., i.v.) and note the administration time.
Place the animal in the activity chamber at the specified time post-administration (e.g., 30 minutes after oral administration).
Start the digital count timer in the photoactometer immediately.
Record the number of photobeam interruptions for each specified observation interval (typically 5 or 10 minute periods; total session 30–60 minutes).
Note the count on the digital display at the end of each interval and reset for the next interval if using cumulative mode.
Observe and record any qualitative behaviours (grooming, rearing, stereotypy, sedation, ataxia).
At the end of the session, remove the animal and return to its cage.
Record total counts, interval counts, and behavioural observations in the laboratory data sheet.
Clean the chamber thoroughly with 70% ethanol between animals.
Analyze data statistically: compare drug group vs. control group using unpaired t-test or ANOVA.
precautions: Ensure background lighting is consistent for all animals — photobeam-based activity measurement is sensitive to ambient light changes.
Perform all experiments at the same time of day — rodent locomotor activity follows a circadian rhythm.
Acclimatize animals adequately — stress from handling inflates baseline activity counts.
Use the same handler for all animals in a study to minimize inter-handler stress variability.
Clean chambers between animals — olfactory cues from previous animals significantly alter behaviour.
Keep the room quiet during recording — sudden sounds increase activity counts artificially.
Follow CPCSEA and IAEC guidelines for use of laboratory animals.
